Global measles deaths hit a historic low in 2025, the World Health Organization said on Friday, although millions of children still missed vaccinations and outbreaks persisted in dozens of countries.The UN health agency estimated 9.8 million measles cases and about 72,000 deaths worldwide in 2025 - down 74% from 37.8 million cases in 2000, with deaths falling roughly 91% from about 769,000.

WHO said global measles immunization rates remained largely unchanged in 2025, but cautioned the trend hides declines in some regions, including the Americas, where coverage has dropped from levels above 90% before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Advt

Several countries have recently lost their measles elimination status, showing that without high vaccination coverage, surveillance and political will, the virus can "quickly regain a foothold," WHO said.

Twenty-nine million children were unvaccinated or under-vaccinated against measles in 2025, the agency said on a press call. WHO estimated that 20.8 million infants missed a first dose of vaccine and another 8.3 million missed a second dose."The recent setbacks we've seen are not a failure of the measles vaccine, they're a failure to reach every child with the vaccine," said Dr. Kate O'Brien, director of WHO's Department of Immunization, Vaccines and Biologicals.

WHO said 59 countries reported large or disruptive outbreaks in 2025, compared with 61 in 2024 and 58 in 2023.CALL FOR INVESTMENTO'Brien called for countries to "double down on the investments in their programs," to ensure that the vaccine is available at times and places that people can easily access.WHO warned that immunization and surveillance programmes face increasing financial pressures even as the costs of closing immunity gaps and responding to outbreaks rise.

O'Brien said the measles vaccine delivers one of the highest returns on investment of any vaccine, calling it "a best buy."
